newsitem.title: JAPAN: KDD cuts rates to boost international position.
newsitem.headline: KDD cuts rates to boost international position.

text.p: Japanese telecommunications giant Kokusai Denshin Denwa Co Ltd announced more rate cuts on Thursday, trying to stay one step ahead of a growing crowd of competitors.
Analysts say the moves will help it cope amid an imminent shake-up in the industry, but the international operator's future is still anything but rosy.
The former government-owned company said on Thursday that it plans to cut its international phone charges by an average of 5.1 percent from November 23.
"This is aimed at strengthening our international position at a time of drastic changes in the global market environment," KDD president Tadashi Nishimoto told a news conference.
"Our rates are now a lot cheaper than those offered by American call-back operators," said Nishimoto, denying criticism that the firm charges much higher rates than its foreign competitors.
KDD, which is already gradually losing its market share in Japan's international phone market, faces growing competition from foreign and domestic competitors.
Some analysts question whether KDD can remain on top.
"KDD is burdened with high personnel and investment costs and the prospects are not rosy," said Hironobu Sawake, analyst at Nikko Research Centre.
Recent media reports that U.S. telephone operator AT&T Corp would offer discount call-back services in Japan sparked talk that KDD would lose sales to its U.S. competitor.
"An attack by such a huge company with abundant funds has raised concerns if any of Japan's international operators can survive," said an official at an international telephone operator.
AT&T, which boasts revenues 10 times larger to that of KDD, declined to comment on the media reports.
But whether or not AT&T enters the Japanese market, price competition with foreign giants is certain to heat up next year.

By the end of next year, Japan will deregulate the market for international leased phone lines. This will allow foreign telecommunications operators that do not have local call networks in Japan to launch international services at relatively low cost.
KDD's troubles are also likely to come from the domestic market too. Japan's powerful Nippon Telegraph and Telephone Corp wants to start international services.
Analysts say if that it does launch services, global telecommunications alliances, such as British Telecommunications and MCI's Concert, will rush to seek partnerships with NTT.
"KDD will continue to face heavy rate cut pressure, but the question is how to make up for lower revenues and profits stemming from rate cuts," said Nikko's Sawake.

KDD announced lower half-year results on Thursday, suffering an 18.3 percent year-on-year drop in parent current profits to 14.49 billion yen ($130 million), because of rate cuts implemented in June 1996 and November 1995.
It forecasts 24 billion yen ($216 million) in full-year parent current profits, against a 31.25 billion yen ($281 million) profit a year ago. ($1=111 yen)
